You use Perfect Infinitives in two ways:
1. After link verbs (seem and appear) to refer to a previous time period

For example:
There seems to have been some sort of mistake.
The matter appears to have been resolved.
1. After phrases expressing emotions and feelings

For example:
I'm sorry to have kept you waiting for so long.
She was happy to have met the hiring requirements.
The structure of the Perfect infinitive is:
I'm sorry to have kept you waiting.
I plan to have selected several more topics before our next staff meeting.
There seems to have been some misunderstanding about that.
Reporting and Commenting: The Present Perfect Tense
You can use the Present Perfect with verbs like reckon, imagine and suppose when you want to comment or report on what has been done.

When you use the Present Perfect, you refer to things that happened in the past but have a connection to the present.
This is useful when you talk about how things affect you and your current situation.

For example:
I reckon you have won the most valuable employee award.
I imagine you have seen from my resumé that I worked as a copy editor and proofreader at a campus newspaper, where I also sell advertising space.
I suppose you have established a great working relationship.
You use the past participle of the main verb in the Present Perfect tense.

images.text:
Adam: Hi Kristi! How's it going?
Kristi: Good thanks, I'm sorry to have kept you waiting. How have you been?
Adam: Not bad. I hardly ever see you. I imagine you have been sent to a lot of different places recently.
Kristi: Yes, I suppose they have decided to keep me busy.
Adam: I read your awesome blog about grammar. Very interesting!
Kristi: Thanks! When it comes to writers, grammar really separates the wheat from the chaff. Some reports seem to flow well and may appear easy to understand, while others seem more laborious to read. You need to write clearly to be successful in business. Often, the difference lies in the use of grammar.

Adam: That would lies, L - I - E - S, or lays, L - A - Y - S?
Kristi: That would be L - I - E - S, because that is a different meaning of the verb to lie. It also means "to have a place."
Adam: Do you have any more ideas for blogs?
Kristi: Not yet, but I plan to have selected several more topics before our next staff meeting. I'm interested in inquiring into about how English is changing due to international trade.
Adam: Really?
Kristi: All languages change, but I imagine English has earned a reputation for changing faster than other languages. For example, anymore is a word that used to only be used in negative sentences like I don't drink coffee anymore. Now, it's being used in positive sentences, like I've been drinking a lot of coffee anymore. Now, it also means something similar to lately.

Adam: Don't you think people should use correct English?
Kristi: There seems to have been some misunderstanding about that. I guess when people say "correct English", they have usually meant Standard English. Standard English is actually just one dialect of English. Every dialect has rules. These rules tell us what language is like rather than what it should be like. This is called the normative approach to grammar.
Adam: I reckon my old grammar teacher has not heard about that.
Kristi: Maybe she has, by now!
